newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Spanish buyouts underline Argentine bank prospects.
newsitem.headline: Spanish buyouts underline Argentine bank prospects.

text.p: The second purchase of an Argentine bank by a Spanish financial institution in as many weeks underlines the huge potential for growth in the sector and strong confidence in the Argentine economy, analysts said.

Spain's Banco Santander SA on Tuesday said it would pay $594 million for 35.06 percent of Argentina's Banco Rio de la Plata's share capital with an option for an additional 15 percent. The stake provides voting control of the bank.

It is "certainly a sign of confidence," in the potential for growth in Arentina's banking sector, said Daniel Tassan-Din, head of research and banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Buenos Aires.

He suggested the "potential for expansion of banking services in Argentina is greater than anywhere else in Latin America," because of the strong growth in the economy and the rapidly increasing deposits in the banking system.
Bank deposits rose to $59 billion in March from $50 billion a year earlier.
"The potential pie of credit is very big," said Nuno Fernandes, Latin American bank analyst at ING Barings in New York.

Bank deposits are currently equal to 22 percent of gross domestic product in Argentina, compared with 30 percent in Brazil, 37 percent in Chile and 44 percent in Mexico, suggesting ample room for growth.

Analysts said that may have been uppermost in Spain's Banco de Bilbao Viscaya's mind when its Argentine-controlled Banco Frances two weeks ago bought 71.8 percent of retail bank Banco de Credito Argentino.

That expansion will serve to extend BBV's retail banking services at a stroke -- something that puts BBV in a better position to benefit from expansion in the consumer banking segment, the area Tassan-Din thinks has the best prospects for growth in coming years.

Deutsche Morgan's Tassan-Din said Santander would not bring Rio quite as many benefits through its purchase because Santander does not bring an enlarged retail network to Rio. Santander in Argentina has more emphasis on brokerage activities although it is active in the pension funds business.

Most importantly though, the increasing participation of foreign banks in Argentina's banking sector will serve to bring more competition, something that should eventually lead to reductions in fees and lower administration costs.
"It is a very healthy process and absolutely necessary to be on a competitive level with other economies," said Rodolfo Rossi, former president of Argentina's central bank.

Certainly the entry of large international banks in the local system will contribute to the solidity of the banking sector, as it will make Argentine banks less vulnerable to external shocks such as the so-called Tequila crisis in 1995, when 20 percent of bank deposits were withdrawn, forcing many banks to shut.
Tassan-Din said any further mergers or buy-outs are highly likely to include Banco de Galicia, the largest remaining Argentine bank without foreign ownership.
There may be no more Iberian banks interested in expanding in Argentina but Citicorp of the United States is a possible candidate in any future acquisition, Tassan-Din added.
Fernandes said there was likely to be some interest from Chilean banks in Argentina when Chile eases its controls on foreign ownersip by its banks.
